name: Measuring Whether Personalization Works
title: Measuring Whether Personalization Works
answer: Personalized learning and tutoring tools should be judged by what students can do independently compared with students who did not use the tool, not by how often they logged in. Results need to be checked more than once, including midyear and at the end, and broken out by student group so that average gains do not hide students falling further behind. Enjoyment of a tool is welcome but is not the same as learning.

sections.body: Personalized learning is simple to describe but difficult to measure, and usage statistics only show that students logged in rather than that they learned. The pilot method from Chapter 4 applies with special force here, meaning every tutoring or personalized learning tool should be judged by what students can do on their own compared with students who did not use it. Motivation also deserves attention, but it can mislead because students often enjoy a new tool and that enjoyment can fade. The problem this solves is the risk of adopting a tool on the strength of engagement or enthusiasm rather than evidence of learning.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the tool is treated as something to test rather than assume, with students who use it compared against students who do not on what they can do independently. Results are checked at more than one point in time, at the middle and end of the year, because a tool that helps in the first month may help less by spring and a tool that seems slow at first may pay off later. Checking twice also gives teachers a chance to adjust how they use the tool. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond the trial described in grades 7 through 9, so the practice applies across the school as a comparison of users and non users.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea through the pilot method and reports one specific finding. A trial with 371 students in grades 7 through 9 found that AI tools designed to support motivation and learning strategies did not beat a plain chatbot on effort or knowledge (Futterer et al., 2026). The text uses this finding to make the point that enjoyment is welcome but is not the same as learning, and that motivation data can mislead. No other study, figure or finding is given for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that usage statistics do not show learning, that enjoyment can fade and is not the same as learning, and that an average gain can hide students who are falling further behind. When results differ by student group, the district should ask why and adjust, because personalized learning that helps only some students is not doing its job. The decisions that stay with people are the choice of what to measure, when to check results, how to break them out by group, and how to change practice when the picture is uneven. Nothing here is legal advice, and the text describes practice rather than a rule.
